title: Aircraft Flight Controls and Operation of Systems
summary: Trace what each control changes, where each instrument gets information, and which failures share a common cause.
objectives: Relate primary controls, coordination, trim, and configuration changes to aerodynamic effects.
Trace power, fuel, ignition, electrical, and instrument information paths.
Identify aircraft-specific details that must come from the actual AFM/POH and equipment supplements.

sections.title: Axes, control surfaces, and coordination
sections.body:
Ailerons primarily command roll about the longitudinal axis. Elevator or stabilator input changes pitching moment about the lateral axis. Rudder primarily commands yaw about the vertical axis. The flight path changes through the resulting forces; a pitch input is not a direct promise of climb, and yaw alone is not the normal way to generate a coordinated turn.

During roll entry, asymmetric wing drag can yaw the nose opposite the intended bank. Appropriate rudder coordinates the maneuver. In an established turn, control requirements change with aircraft characteristics and flight condition. Watch the airplane’s response rather than applying the same pedal position from entry through rollout.
sections.deep:
Why the rudder has more than one job: it manages yaw and sideslip during turns, but also supports crosswind control, intentional slips, asymmetric-thrust handling, and some recovery procedures. A slip can be deliberate and useful when allowed by the aircraft procedures; it is not automatically an error. A skid near a stall is a different and potentially serious condition.

Use the inclinometer and outside picture appropriately. A centered ball is coordination information; the miniature aircraft in a conventional turn coordinator is principally rate information, not a substitute attitude indicator. Teach a light, controlled grip so the student can sense pressure changes without repeatedly overcorrecting.

sections.title: Trim, flaps, and secondary controls
sections.body:
Trim relieves the sustained control force required for a chosen condition. Establish the desired attitude, power, and configuration, then remove the unwanted pressure. Re-trim when speed, power, or configuration changes. Trying to fly an entire correction with the trim wheel can delay control and hide an unsuitable flight condition.

Flaps change wing geometry. They can increase maximum lift coefficient, reduce stall speed, add drag, and alter pitching moment. The balance varies with flap design and deflection. Slats and slots can delay separation by influencing the upper-surface flow. Spoilers reduce lift and often increase drag; their purposes and permitted use depend on the aircraft.
sections.deep:
Why a trim tab can move opposite the elevator: a conventional tab uses aerodynamic force on a small surface to create a balancing moment on the larger one. Other aircraft use stabilator anti-servo tabs, adjustable stabilizers, springs, or different mechanisms. Learn the installed design before predicting movement or failure behavior.

Respect flap-extension speeds, configuration restrictions, and electric-trim/autopilot procedures. A ground-adjustable rudder tab is a rigging item, not an in-flight pilot control or an invitation to bend hardware casually. Obtain qualified maintenance guidance. The correct trim result is manageable control force, not hands-off proof that the aircraft will hold altitude indefinitely.

sections.title: Piston engines, ignition, and propellers
sections.body:
A four-stroke reciprocating engine draws in a charge, compresses it, burns it to produce work, and expels exhaust. Many trainers use air-cooled, horizontally opposed engines with dual magneto ignition. A conventional magneto generates its own ignition energy, so loss of the aircraft alternator does not by itself stop that ignition. Electronically controlled or differently installed engines may have different dependencies.

A fixed-pitch propeller has a blade-angle compromise; its rpm responds to power and flight condition. A constant-speed system uses a governor to vary blade pitch and maintain the selected rpm while it remains within the governing range. Blade stops and system limits prevent unlimited compensation.
sections.deep:
Why: each blade section is an airfoil. Its angle of attack depends on rotational speed, forward speed, and geometric pitch. If rpm tends to rise in a normal governing condition, the governor generally commands more blade loading by increasing pitch. If rpm tends to fall, it generally commands less. The exact oil-pressure and failure-to-pitch behavior depends on the installation.

Use the aircraft’s approved sequence for power, propeller, and mixture changes. “Every C172 has the same engine” is false: model, serial range, modifications, and supplements matter. Identify the engine and propeller actually installed before teaching their normal and emergency procedures.

sections.title: Fuel, induction, oil, and supporting systems
sections.body:
Trace fuel from each tank through vents, selector, drains, pumps, metering, and injectors or carburetor. A high wing may provide gravity assistance, but that does not establish that every operating condition is independent of pumps or tank selection. Vent blockage, contamination, a wrong selector position, and an empty tank create different problems even when fuel remains elsewhere aboard.

Carburetors and fuel-injection systems meter fuel differently. Carburetor icing can occur without visible structural ice; a fuel-injected engine avoids the carburetor’s particular icing mechanism but can still suffer induction blockage or other icing. Mixture management must follow the actual engine and POH guidance.
sections.deep:
Why oil matters: oil lubricates, carries heat, helps sealing, and carries contaminants to filtration or collection points. Depending on installation, it may also operate a propeller mechanism or other components. Pressure and temperature are related but distinct clues; neither should be dismissed because the other appears normal.

Tank capacities, usable fuel, minimum oil, approved grades, pump operation, and hydraulic-fluid types are aircraft-specific. A 172R, 172S, older carbureted 172, or modified airplane need not match a slide’s figures. Use the approved systems description and limitations for that aircraft. Color is a useful leak clue only after identifying the fluid and installation.

sections.title: Electrical supply and shared failure paths
sections.body:
An alternator supplies electrical power and normally supports battery charging. The battery can provide starting energy and a limited reserve after a generating-system failure. A nominal 24-volt battery may operate in a nominal 28-volt charging system, but those labels are not universal aircraft specifications. The approved system voltage, alternator capacity, bus arrangement, and reserve duration come from the aircraft documentation.

After an alternator failure, electrical equipment may appear normal initially because the battery is still supplying it. Follow the aircraft checklist to identify the problem, manage loads, and select a suitable landing plan. An illuminated display is not evidence that the charging system is healthy.
sections.deep:
Why redundancy needs a diagram: two displays may share a bus, sensor, antenna, or power source. A backup that fails from the same single cause is not fully independent. Conversely, a conventional magneto-powered engine can continue running while radios or electrically driven instruments lose their supply.

Trace the installed autopilot’s power, attitude, air-data, trim, and disengagement paths. Know what its annunciations mean and how a failure changes control responsibility. Do not infer G5, G1000, vacuum, or backup-battery behavior from a generic cockpit picture. Equipment supplements belong in the same teaching discussion as the main POH.

sections.title: Pressure instruments and blockage patterns
sections.body:
The airspeed indicator compares pitot total pressure with static pressure. Their difference relates to dynamic pressure and therefore airspeed. The altimeter senses static pressure using nearly evacuated aneroid elements and a calibrated mechanism. The altimeter setting adjusts the reference; the wafers are not simply containers permanently filled to 29.92 inches of mercury. A conventional vertical-speed indicator compares prompt static-pressure change with pressure delayed by a calibrated restriction.

This shared plumbing explains shared symptoms. A blocked static source can freeze the altimeter, drive the VSI toward zero, and cause airspeed errors as altitude changes. A pitot blockage mainly affects the airspeed indication.
sections.deep:
Trace the trapped pressure: if the pitot inlet is blocked while its drain remains open, the airspeed reading normally falls toward zero. If both inlet and drain are blocked but static remains available, trapped pitot pressure can make the airspeed indication rise in a climb and fall in a descent. With static blocked and pitot clear, a climb above the blockage altitude generally makes the airspeed read too low.

These are idealized diagnostic patterns, not a license to continue by mental correction. Use the installed alternate-static, pitot-heat, and unreliable-airspeed procedures. Cabin alternate-static pressure can differ from outside pressure, so apply the published corrections and limitations.

sections.title: Gyros, landing gear, and ice protection
sections.body:
Conventional attitude and heading gyros use rigidity in space; a turn-rate instrument uses gyroscopic response to rotation. Vacuum and electrical power sources vary by installation. Modern AHRS and electronic displays may replace the spinning gyros, but they still depend on sensors, power, and a validated attitude solution. Cross-check indications against genuinely independent references.

Retractable landing gear adds actuation, indication, interlocks, and an emergency-extension method. A selector position does not prove the gear reached the commanded state. Fixed gear removes the retraction system but does not remove inspection or brake-system responsibilities. Learn the installed gear’s indications and approved abnormal procedure.
sections.deep:
Ice protection: anti-ice aims to prevent accumulation or bonding; deice removes accumulated ice. Actual equipment may combine functions. Pitot heat protects a pressure source; it does not make the wing or the whole airplane approved for flight in icing. A warm windshield likewise does not establish an icing authorization.

Identify protected surfaces, activation limits, power demands, failure cues, and the AFM/POH icing limitation. Ice can alter the wing, tail, propeller, engine induction, and instruments in different ways. Treat a generic systems lesson as a map for finding the aircraft-specific answers, not as a substitute for those answers.

teachBack: Trace how a power change can require both coordination and new elevator trim.
Using the actual POH, identify which engine functions survive a complete aircraft electrical failure.
Draw the pitot/static connections, then predict a blockage’s effect before looking at a memorized table.
takeaways: Controls create moments and forces; the flight path follows the resulting energy and aerodynamic state.
Trim reduces force after the desired condition is established.
A backup can share the same failure source as the primary.
Pressure-instrument errors follow the pressure that is trapped or lost.
Use the actual model, serial applicability, and supplements for system numbers and procedures.

quiz.question: A conventional dual-magneto trainer loses alternator output. Why may its engine continue while battery-powered avionics eventually stop?
options: The magnetos and avionics both have unlimited battery reserve.
The propeller supplies electrical power to every instrument.
The magnetos generate ignition energy independently of the aircraft charging system.
The alternator is required only while the starter is engaged.
feedback: The avionics depend on a finite electrical reserve and magnetos do not rely on it in the stated installation.
Propeller rotation does not provide a universal independent supply for all instruments.
The stated magneto installation can keep providing spark while electrical equipment draws down the battery.
The alternator normally supplies ongoing aircraft electrical loads after starting.
quiz.hint: Separate the ignition-energy path from the avionics supply path.

quiz.question: The pitot inlet becomes blocked, its drain remains open, and the static source remains clear. What airspeed-indicator behavior is expected in the ideal case?
options: The reading falls toward zero.
The reading becomes an accurate groundspeed display.
The indication freezes permanently at the original value.
The altimeter must immediately indicate sea level.
feedback: The pitot pressure vents toward ambient pressure, eliminating the normal measured pressure difference.
The airspeed instrument does not acquire ground-reference information from this failure.
The open drain prevents the simple trapped-total-pressure condition.
The altimeter uses static pressure, which remains available in this scenario.
quiz.hint: Determine whether total pressure is trapped or allowed to vent.

quiz.question: The static source becomes completely blocked during a climb while the pitot inlet remains clear. Which combination best matches the ideal pattern?
options: Altimeter rises normally, VSI shows a larger climb, and ASI is unchanged.
Altimeter freezes, VSI settles toward zero, and ASI tends to underread above the blockage altitude.
Every instrument drops immediately to zero.
Only the heading indicator changes.
feedback: All three pressure instruments use the static source, so normal altitude and vertical-speed behavior is not expected.
Trapped static pressure freezes altitude reference and biases the airspeed comparison as the aircraft climbs.
The trapped static pressure is not zero, and the instruments respond differently to it.
A conventional heading indicator does not use static pressure as its heading source.
quiz.hint: Follow the same trapped static pressure into all three instruments.

quiz.question: Within the normal governing range, a constant-speed propeller begins tending toward an rpm above the selected value. What general governor action opposes that tendency?
options: Decrease blade pitch to reduce propeller loading.
Retract the landing gear to reduce drag.
Increase mixture richness as the sole rpm control.
Increase blade pitch to increase propeller loading.
feedback: Lower pitch generally reduces propeller loading and would not oppose the stated overspeed tendency.
Landing-gear drag is not the governor’s blade-angle control mechanism.
Mixture is not the propeller governor’s normal means of maintaining selected rpm.
A greater blade angle generally adds load, opposing the rise in rpm within the governing range.
quiz.hint: Think about the torque required to turn the propeller after changing blade angle.

quiz.question: A slide lists a particular C172’s usable fuel and minimum preflight oil quantity. Before applying those figures to another C172, what should the instructor verify?
options: Only that both airplanes have high wings.
The installed aircraft’s applicable POH/AFM, model, modifications, and supplements.
That both fuel selectors have the same color.
That a previous renter recalls using those amounts.
feedback: Wing arrangement does not establish the engine, tank capacity, or operating limitations.
Those records establish which system and operating numbers actually apply.
Selector appearance does not verify system capacity or approved limitations.
A recollection is not the governing aircraft-specific source.
quiz.hint: Identify the source that establishes applicability, rather than similarity.

quiz.question: An airplane has pitot heat and windshield defrost but no approved icing authorization. What follows?
options: It can safely remain in icing if both switches are on.
Pitot heat protects every air-data and aerodynamic surface.
The wing and tail can still accumulate hazardous ice, so the equipment does not establish icing approval.
Windshield visibility alone determines the aircraft’s icing capability.
feedback: Those devices do not establish protection of the whole aircraft or an authorization.
Pitot heat addresses a local pressure-source hazard rather than all exposed surfaces and sensors.
Local equipment capability and whole-aircraft icing approval are different determinations.
A clear windshield does not show the aerodynamic condition of the wing or tail.
quiz.hint: Separate the protected component from the aircraft’s operating limitation.
